context_blurb:
Water, soil, sunlight, wind, forests, metals, coal and oil all come from nature, and people use them every day. They are called natural resources. Some come back soon after they are used, the way a forest grows again. Others take so long to form that, once they are used, nature will not make more for ages.

If nature replaces a resource within the span of a person's life, it is renewable. If nature takes far longer, it is nonrenewable. Coal is nonrenewable: it takes millions of years to form underground, so the coal burned today will not be replaced within anyone's lifetime. Oil and natural gas are nonrenewable for the same reason. Trees grow back within decades and a new corn crop grows every year, so firewood and fuel made from corn are renewable. The moving water that turns a dam's wheels is not used up at all, since rain and snow keep the river full.

Metals come from rock as well. Copper, the metal in many water pipes and wires, is dug from rocks called ores. Copper is nonrenewable, like other metals, because nature takes millions of years to make new copper ore, far too slowly for any human life. Used copper can be recycled again and again, as good as new. That makes the copper already dug up last longer, but it does not make copper renewable. Copper does not rust, either: over many years it grows a thin green coat that protects the metal beneath.

Soil is a resource too. Topsoil is made of rock broken down into tiny grains, mixed with the rotted remains of plants and animals. Nature makes it very slowly: a layer one inch deep, about two and a half centimetres, takes hundreds of years to form, from a few hundred to about a thousand. That is far longer than a human life. Rain and wind often carry topsoil away faster than it forms.

Plastic is made in factories, not found in nature. More than ninety percent of plastic is made from oil and natural gas, so most plastic comes from nonrenewable fuels. Less than one percent comes from plants.

Aluminium, the metal of drink cans, comes from a rock called bauxite. Making aluminium from old cans takes only about five percent of the energy needed to make it from bauxite, so recycling saves almost all of it, about ninety-five percent. Each tonne of recycled aluminium also leaves about four tonnes of bauxite in the ground.

Paper is made of tiny fibres from trees, and every time paper goes through recycling, its fibres get a little shorter and weaker, so it slowly wears out. In the end, fresh fibres must be mixed in; people often say this happens after about five to seven trips. Glass and metals are different: they are melted and remade, and they can go round again and again without wearing out. Thin kitchen foil tears as easily as paper, but it is aluminium, remade just like a can.

People speak of three Rs: reduce, reuse and recycle. Reducing means using less of something. Reusing means using a thing again just as it is, without breaking it down, such as filling an empty jam jar with buttons. Recycling means breaking a used thing down and making its material into something new, the way old cans become new ones.

Conserving a resource means using less of it and wasting less, which is the same as reducing. A family that fixes a dripping tap, takes showers rather than baths and sweeps the steps rather than hosing them is conserving water, because each of those jobs uses less.

Plastic left outdoors lasts a long time. Bacteria and fungi break down almost none of it, so it does not rot away like old leaves. Instead, sunlight makes it brittle, and the weather cracks it into tiny bits of plastic. Two scientists, Imogen Napper and Richard Thompson, tested this: they left plastic bags out in the open air, and within nine months every bag had fallen to pieces. The bits can last for decades or even centuries. More than 700 kinds of animals have been found to swallow plastic, often mistaking it for food.
